sentence: I clicked one link to read one article and the site has now spawned three pop-ups, two overlays, a video player that has docked to the bottom of the screen, and a newsletter signup form that covers the bottom half of the article. The article itself is four paragraphs long. The pop-ups are more numerous than the paragraphs. The site has prioritized harvesting my attention over delivering what I came for.

Save your money. This contractor will quote you a fair price, take a fifty percent deposit, demolish half your kitchen, and then add forty thousand dollars of surprise costs before he will finish the job. Every neighbor on my block has the same story. He is well-known in the area for this exact tactic. The state licensing board has been notified, the better business bureau has been notified, and now you are being notified. Walk away. Run.

I have just watched the gate agent change my boarding zone from group one to group four with no explanation. The boarding pass on my phone updated automatically. The new boarding zone means I will not get overhead bin space. I will be forced to check my carry-on at the gate. The carry-on contains my laptop, my passport, and my medication. The agent has informed me I can opt to wait and see if there is room. The wait will be ten minutes after the door closes. The flight leaves in fifteen.

I am not going to keep covering for your missed deadlines while you take long lunches and disappear from Slack for three hours at a time. The work is not getting done because you are not doing it. I am not your assistant. I am not your safety net. The next time something blows up because you ghosted a deliverable, I am letting it blow up, and I am pointing directly at the source.

I have asked you three times to stop reply-all-ing to threads that do not concern you, and yet here we are again, watching you weigh in on a project you are not on, were never invited to, and have no business commenting about. Read the room. Read the email chain. Read literally anything other than the sound of your own voice in your head telling you that everyone wants your unsolicited opinion. They do not. I do not. Stop.

The guy doing curls in the squat rack is the universal symbol of gym incompetence. There are sixteen other stations where you could perform that exercise. You chose the one piece of equipment that exists specifically for compound lifts no other equipment can replace. Either you do not understand what a squat rack is for, or you do not care that other people exist. Either way, I am out of patience.

Your habit of marking every email urgent and every meeting critical has rendered the words meaningless. Nothing you send is actually time-sensitive. Nothing you propose actually matters. You are crying wolf so loudly and so often that the entire department has tuned you out. The fact that you do not realize this, and continue to escalate, is genuinely embarrassing to watch. Calm down. Nothing is on fire.

He called me at nine forty-five on a Friday night to ask about a slide in a deck that is not due until Wednesday. There was no emergency. There was no client request. There was no contextual reason for the call. He was at home, drinking, scrolling through the deck on his phone, and decided he wanted to bother me. The disregard for boundaries is staggering. I am supposed to drop my evening to discuss formatting with a man who cannot leave work at work.

Within twenty-four hours of the apology, the company released a positive earnings report and the stock jumped. The market does not care. The board does not care. The customers, who are supposed to be the moral compass of these organizations, did not vote with their feet because the alternative is a different company that will do the same thing and apologize the same way next year. The entire ecosystem is rotted through.

Do not call back. Do not transfer me. Do not have your manager call back. I do not want to hear from your company in any form, ever, again. The next call results in a formal complaint to my state attorney general. I have done my homework. I know the relevant statutes. I am not bluffing. The audacity of cold-calling people in twenty twenty-six should be a class C misdemeanor and I will work tirelessly to make it one.

The kitchen has had ninety minutes to produce two sandwiches. Two. Bread, filling, bread. A child could assemble this in under three. When I asked about the status of our order the server gave me an apologetic shrug and disappeared into the back, where I imagine the chef is conducting a leisurely tutorial on knife skills while our food cools on the pass. We are leaving without paying. The manager can chase us if he wishes.

The guy who slammed his weights down so hard the entire building shook should be banned for life. There is no version of strength training that requires you to drop forty-five-pound plates from chest height onto a thin layer of rubber flooring. You are not impressive. You are loud. You are a liability for the gym's insurance. And you are ruining the workout of every single person within sixty feet of your spectacle.

I have filed twelve noise complaints in three months. The neighbors continue to host parties that vibrate the walls until four in the morning. The property manager has spoken to them, as he tells me each time, but the conversations have produced no behavioral change. The police were called twice and responded by knocking once and leaving. The HOA has decided that this falls outside their jurisdiction. Every authority has agreed that the problem is real and that solving it is not their job.

Reality television has done more damage to the public's ability to communicate calmly than any other force I can think of. People now believe that shouting over each other, throwing drinks, and storming out of rooms is the normal way to handle disagreement. Three generations of viewers have absorbed this as the cultural default. It is corrosive. It is exhausting. And the producers laugh all the way to the bank while we burn down the social contract.

The update notes claim performance improvements. The app is now demonstrably slower than the previous version. The update notes claim bug fixes. The bugs from the last three versions remain unaddressed and new ones have been introduced. The update notes claim improved stability. The app has crashed three times since installation. The update notes are lies. The update notes have been lies since the dawn of this product line.

The first twenty pages are unreadable. The next two hundred are merely tedious. The final hundred try to redeem the whole exercise with a twist that has been telegraphed since chapter two. The author thinks she is being clever. She is not being clever. She is being predictable while wearing the costume of cleverness, and the difference is obvious to anyone who has read more than three novels in their life. Pass.

Five outages this week and the support chat keeps blaming weather. There is no weather. It is sixty-eight degrees and sunny. The sky is empty. Stop telling me about weather. The problem is your equipment, which has been failing on a weekly basis since I signed up, and your refusal to send a technician until I have spent two hours on chat with someone reading from a script written by someone who has never used the internet.

The receipt is printing. It has been printing for two minutes. It is now two feet long and continuing. It contains coupons, surveys, rewards offers, a cartoon mascot, and a printed apology from corporate for inconvenience. I do not want any of this. I want my receipt to confirm that I have paid and to free me from this physical building. The dot matrix sputter mocks me. I am owed compensation for the time I spent watching paper unspool.

I have been shadowbanned for three months on a platform I use professionally. No explanation. No notification. Just a steady decline in reach and engagement until I figured out what was happening from a forum post. The appeals process is a black hole. The customer support is an automated email that thanks me for my patience. I am one of millions in the same situation, and the platform pretends none of us exist. Pure corporate indifference.

The apology video was filmed in soft lighting with sad music playing under the executive's voice. He paused for effect. He looked into the camera with practiced sincerity. His tie was carefully chosen to look subdued but not funereal. Every element of this performance was workshopped. There was nothing spontaneous, nothing human, nothing real. It was a commercial for contrition produced by people who have never felt any.

The light at the top of the off-ramp turns green for exactly four seconds before turning red again, and there is a line of fifty cars trying to make it through. Whoever programmed this signal is either incompetent or sadistic. I sit through that light six times most mornings, watching the same green flash mock me from a hundred yards away, and slowly losing my will to participate in modern civilization.

I am tired of being lectured by people whose only credential is having found a personal eating routine that worked for them. Anecdote is not data. Your six-month transformation is not a peer-reviewed study. The fact that something worked for you, in your body, with your genetics, does not mean it will work for everyone, and the relentless evangelism about how it should is exhausting and harmful and needs to stop.

The weather app is reading my SMS messages. The weather. App. Is reading. My text messages. The justification, buried in the privacy policy, is that text messages may contain weather-related information that helps personalize the experience. No one texts me weather. No one has ever texted me weather. The justification is a fig leaf the size of a postage stamp, attempting to cover a permission grab the size of a barn door.

It is two o'clock on a Tuesday afternoon and I am parked on the highway. Parked. Not slow, not crawling, parked. There is no game, no event, no holiday, no excuse for this except the city's refusal to invest in infrastructure for forty years while real estate developers built thirty thousand new condos along the corridor. The whole system is broken and everyone responsible should be voted out.

I clicked on a news article and immediately seven ads loaded above the fold, two of them autoplay videos with sound, one of them a pop-up demanding I subscribe to a newsletter, and one of them a survey about my satisfaction with the site I have been on for exactly four seconds. I came here to read about local elections. I have now navigated three close buttons, muted one video, and accepted seventy-three different cookies. The article itself is fifty words long.

The heater has been broken since November. It is now February. I have been wearing a winter coat indoors for three months while you tell me the part is on order. The part has never been on order. The part does not exist. You are stalling because fixing the heater costs money and your business model is built on doing as little as possible while collecting as much as possible. I see you. The whole building sees you.

The driver rang the doorbell, waited zero seconds, and left a note saying no one was home. I was home. I was walking down the stairs. I opened the door three seconds after the bell rang. The van was already pulling out of the driveway. The note instructs me to drive eleven miles to a depot to pick up my own package, between hours that do not align with my work schedule, by Friday, or the package will be returned. This is not delivery. This is dropping off a homework assignment.

I am trying to write the word definitely and the autocomplete keeps changing it to defiantly. The two words mean entirely different things. I have corrected this ten times in the last paragraph. The autocomplete has learned, somehow, that I prefer defiantly. I do not prefer defiantly. I have never used defiantly in my life. The autocomplete is rewriting my personality from the bottom up, one word at a time, and I am too tired to stop it.

The VAR system was supposed to fix officiating. It has made it worse. Every game now stops for three-minute reviews of plays that were clear to everyone except the booth. The flow of the game is destroyed. The crowd is disengaged. And half the time the on-field decision is upheld anyway, which raises the obvious question of why we are watching this whole charade in the first place. Useless technology in the hands of useless people.

Stop sending me letters about my trash bin. The bin is in the place it has always been, the place the previous owner used, the place every neighbor on the street uses, and the place that nothing in the bylaws actually prohibits. You have invented a violation in your head and decided I am the convenient target this month. Find a different hobby. Take up gardening. Stop weaponizing the HOA against your neighbors.

The customer service line is a thirty-seven minute hold for a robot to tell me that all agents are busy and I should call back later. Call back later from where? The airport floor I am currently sleeping on? The hotel I cannot afford to book because you have not approved my voucher? Your help line is a polite system for ignoring the customers you have already stranded. I see it for what it is. I see all of it.

The pasta was undercooked, drowning in some unholy gray sauce that tasted like someone had wrung out a dishrag into the bowl. The waiter rolled his eyes when I asked for water, as if hydration were a personal affront to him. I have eaten gas station hot dogs with more dignity than whatever insulting performance was happening in that kitchen. Forty-three dollars for the privilege of being condescended to by a man in a stained apron. Absolute disgrace.

The board hired a lawyer to send me a cease-and-desist over my chicken coop. My chicken coop. I have four hens. They are not loud. They are not visible from the street. They are not bothering anyone. The lawyer cost me three hundred dollars to respond to. The HOA spent ten times that to send the letter. We are all paying for this absurd theater out of our dues. The board should be liable personally, not the community.

The shredder is full of junk mail. The recycling bin is full of junk mail. The trash is full of junk mail. I spend twenty minutes a week processing paper that exists only to advertise products I will never buy. The mailroom is a one-way pipe of corporate effluent flowing into my home and I have no faucet to close.

The home team gets every single call. Every. Single. Call. The away team breathes wrong and it is a foul. The home team commits an obvious infraction and the whistle stays in the pocket. The referees are not even hiding the bias anymore. The whole sport has a credibility problem that will not go away until the league actually does something about the consistent, documented favoritism that everyone watching can see in real time.

The flight has been delayed three times, each by ninety minutes, each communicated five minutes after the previous estimated departure had elapsed. The pattern is now clear. The flight is not delayed. The flight has been canceled in slow motion. The airline is dripping the bad news in small doses to avoid triggering rebooking obligations. The gate agent will not confirm cancellation because the system has not officially canceled. The system is gaslighting an entire terminal.

I have read your entire post twice and I am still trying to understand how someone can be so confidently wrong about so many things in such a small number of sentences. Every single claim you made has been debunked publicly for years. Did you spend ten minutes researching this before you decided to inflict your opinion on a forum full of people who actually do this for a living? Sit down. Listen. Read. You have nothing to teach anyone here.

Stop walking through my set. The line of sight in front of the mirror is not a hallway. There are pathways behind me. Use them. Walking directly in front of someone in the middle of an exercise is dangerous and rude. I almost dropped a bar on my foot because you decided your shortest path through the floor was through my squat. The basic awareness this requires is not optional. Develop it.

Why are there school zones with twenty-five mile-per-hour limits active at eight o'clock at night? There is no school. There are no children. There is nothing but empty buildings and a speed trap waiting to ambush exhausted commuters. The cops sit in the parking lot every evening, lined up like vultures, waiting to fine people for driving the speed the road obviously wants to be driven at. Pathetic revenue grab.

The hotel charged a resort fee for amenities I did not use, will not use, and was not informed about at booking. The amenities consisted of access to a pool that was closed, a gym that required a separate reservation, and a beach that is public property. The resort fee is thirty-five dollars a night. The total trip cost has expanded by over two hundred dollars. The hotel claims the fee is standard. Standard for what. For whom. By whose authority. The whole concept is a scam wearing a uniform.

I have been standing in the rebooking line for two hours and fifteen minutes. There are nine people working at the desk and three of them are visibly assisting passengers. The other six are doing something with their computers that does not appear to involve helping the line. The agents who are helping are processing each passenger in twenty-minute increments. The math suggests I will be here past midnight. The flight I was rebooked onto leaves in forty minutes from a different terminal.

The package was marked delivered at 3:47 PM. At 3:47 PM I was standing on the porch, on the phone with my mother, watching the empty driveway. No truck came. No driver appeared. The package was not delivered to my address. It was delivered to someone else, or to no one, or to the back of the truck where it remains, while the tracking system invents a fiction in which my package is in my hands.

I made a reservation three weeks in advance, called yesterday to confirm, arrived ten minutes early, and was told there would be a brief wait. The brief wait is now forty-five minutes long. The hostess will not make eye contact. The bar is full of walk-ins who arrived after us. The reservation system here is apparently theater, a way to make customers feel important right up until the moment they walk through the door.

Phishing emails that impersonate banks should result in actual prison time, with no exceptions for the cybercrime gangs that operate out of jurisdictions where extradition is hard. Every senior who has lost their savings to one of these schemes deserves justice. The whole industry exists because law enforcement has decided it is too hard to prosecute, and the cost of that decision is measured in destroyed lives. Unacceptable.

After three hours on hold, I finally get a representative who tells me there is nothing she can do, as if she works for a charity instead of a multi-billion-dollar corporation that just stranded me in Cleveland for the night. Nothing she can do? Then what exactly is she there for? Decoration? You canceled my flight with no warning, no compensation, no apology, and now you want me to feel sorry for the agent reading from a script? Refund. Now.

The boarding sign at the gate has been displaying the boarding time as five minutes ago for the last forty minutes. No boarding has occurred. No announcement has been made. The agents have left the desk. The plane is allegedly at the gate. The passengers are crowded around the jet bridge entrance in a state of nervous shuffling. We are all watching each other for clues. The airline has abandoned us collectively and is hoping we figure something out.

The error message says please correct the highlighted fields. There are no highlighted fields. Every field looks the same. The error message is referring to something I cannot see. The submit button is grayed out. The page does not scroll to the offending field. The form has decided to be cryptic for sport. There is no help text, no tooltip, no clarifying language. I am supposed to guess. I refuse to guess. I have closed the tab and abandoned the application entirely.

The relative who has never run a business is explaining to me how to run my business. He is providing advice based on a podcast he listened to last week and a book he read part of in 2018. He is delivering it with the certainty of a CEO. The advice is wrong. Some of it is illegal. The rest is impractical. I have tried to redirect the conversation three times. He will not be redirected. He has come prepared with talking points.

The download is at ninety-seven percent and has been at ninety-seven percent for forty-five minutes. The progress bar inches forward by one pixel every few minutes only to inch back. The estimated time remaining oscillates between two minutes and three hours. The fan on my laptop sounds like a small aircraft preparing for departure. The entire machine is being held captive by a process that I cannot see, did not initiate, and cannot cancel.

I went to the new contemporary wing of the museum and walked out within ten minutes. There was a video of an artist eating soup. There was a room with a single fluorescent light. There was a wall labeled untitled. The whole space had been carved out of an old industrial building, and the old industrial building had more aesthetic value than anything anyone had bothered to install in it. Tear it down. Put something real back.

My cousin has decided that my career path is wrong, that my apartment is too small, that my partner is unsuitable, that my haircut is unflattering, and that I should consider moving back home. Her own life is a wreck. She has lost two jobs this year. Her landlord is suing her. Her dog is in the news for biting a delivery driver. The audacity of her offering me advice would be funny if it were not aimed at me. I have stopped responding to her texts.

The construction next door starts at six in the morning, six days a week. The city allows construction to begin at seven. The contractor knows this. The contractor does not care. The complaints I file are routed to a portal that says the issue is under review. Under review for what. The crew is here. They are loud. The hours are written on the permit posted on the fence. There is no review necessary. There is enforcement, which no one is doing.

Real craft has been abandoned for ideas, and the ideas are usually banal. Anyone can have an idea. Few can paint. Few can sculpt. Few can compose. We have decided to celebrate the idea-havers and ignore the makers, and the result is gallery after gallery filled with text-heavy nothing while the museums that actually contain skilled work are dismissed as conservative. It is a generation-long collective tantrum and I am done pretending it is anything else.

The fake tech support that appeared as a popup on my aunt's screen demanded six hundred dollars in gift cards to remove a virus that did not exist. She gave them the gift cards. Her bank could not reverse the transaction. The retailer could not reverse the transaction. The police filed a report and did nothing. Six hundred dollars of a fixed-income retiree's money, gone forever, and the perpetrators are still running the same scam tomorrow morning.

I mentioned that I had been to the doctor and the response was a forty-minute tangent about essential oils, the failures of allopathic medicine, the dangers of vaccines, and the curative properties of a tea sold by a multi-level marketing company my acquaintance has just joined. I did not ask. I do not want the tea. I do not want the lecture. I want to finish my coffee. The unsolicited advice has crossed from annoying into actively dangerous and I am leaving this brunch.

Cancel my account. Today. I do not want to be transferred to retention. I do not want a free upgrade. I do not want a discount that expires in thirty days. I want my account closed and a confirmation number sent to my email immediately. Every minute you spend trying to talk me out of this is another minute I will spend writing the review.

Stop letting your cat into my garden. I have planted flowers there for three years and your cat has destroyed every single one. It digs them up. It uses my mulch as a litter box. It stalks the birds I feed. When I mentioned it to you, you laughed and said cats will be cats. Well, neighbors will be neighbors, and this one is about to install a sprinkler that triggers every time anything four-legged crosses the property line.

I clicked on a setting to turn off notifications and was greeted by a five-step wizard, two upsell screens, a survey about my preferences, and a confirmation dialog asking me three times if I was really sure I wanted to do this. Yes. I am sure. I have been sure for ten minutes. I have lost the will to live in the time it has taken to silence your stupid pop-ups about features I never asked for.

Whoever is running these grandparent scams has stripped my neighbor's mother of every cent she had saved for a nursing home. Her grandson is fine. He was never in trouble. He was never in Mexico. He was never arrested. The whole story was a script. The voice on the phone was an AI imitation. And she is now ninety-one years old, scared, and broke. I would happily testify against the people responsible. Loudly.

The hedge between our yards is on my property. Mine. Not negotiable. You do not get to trim it however you like and certainly do not get to spray it with whatever chemical product turned half of it brown last summer. The fact that you did this without asking, then denied it when I confronted you, is the kind of pettiness I did not think adults engaged in. The fence is going up. Higher than the hedge. Goodbye.

The artist sold a single nonexistent jpeg for sixty-nine million dollars and the auction house clapped like seals. We are in a tulip mania. We are in the middle of one of the most embarrassing speculative bubbles in art history. When it bursts, and it will burst, the people who bought into it will look in the mirror and have to ask themselves what they were thinking. The answer is they were not thinking. They were following each other off a cliff.

The fact that this show has been renewed for a fifth season tells me everything I need to know about the state of modern television. It is a meandering, plot-hole-riddled mess that recycles the same three character beats over and over while the writers congratulate themselves on subverting expectations. There are no expectations left to subvert. There is only the slow, dispiriting realization that no one in the writers room is being held to any standard whatsoever.

Five dollars an hour to park in a lot that was free for three decades is highway robbery, and the meters have been programmed to start clicking the second you arrive, regardless of grace periods that other cities respect. The whole shift to predatory parking enforcement is a revenue grab dressed up as urban policy. We see it. The merchants see it. The whole downtown is dying because nobody wants to risk the gauntlet anymore.

The lead actor delivered every line with the emotional range of a cardboard cutout in a windstorm. The score swelled at moments that were not actually emotional, as if the composer was trying to bully the audience into feeling something. The final twist was telegraphed so heavily in the first ten minutes that I spent the rest of the film hoping I was wrong. I was not. This film is an insult to anyone who paid for it.

The airport sandwich was nineteen dollars. It was a single triangle of soggy bread containing three slivers of turkey and a leaf of wilted lettuce. The vendor smiled at me as if we were not both participating in a hostage situation. The same sandwich exists outside the security cordon for four dollars. The only thing that justifies the difference is that I cannot leave, and they know it, and they have built their entire business model around that knowledge.

Their refund policy is a maze designed to make you give up. The store credit comes with hidden restrictions. The return window is half what the website claims. The customer service representatives are trained to deny, deflect, and delay. After six weeks of escalation I finally got the refund, but I am not the lucky one. Most people gave up. Most people are still out their money. The whole operation is engineered to steal slowly enough that no one notices.

The owner of this gym threatened to sue me when I posted an honest review about the broken equipment. The threat itself proves the review was accurate, because no legitimate business owner would respond to a customer complaint with legal intimidation. Three thousand people saw the original post. Now three thousand people will see this one. And the next one. And every one I write until either the equipment gets fixed or the gym goes out of business. Your move.

Press one for English. Press two for Spanish. Press three to scream into the void. I pressed three and the line went dead, which was the most honest interaction I have had with this company in four years. Their phone tree is not a customer service tool, it is a moat designed to keep customers away from anyone who could actually help. I am done. I am writing a letter. To Congress.

The airline texted me an apology and a fifty-dollar voucher for a future flight on the same airline. The voucher expires in ninety days, cannot be combined with other offers, cannot be used for taxes and fees, and cannot be used during any blackout date, which appears to be most of the next ninety days. The voucher is an insult disguised as a gesture. I will not be flying this airline again, on principle, and the voucher will expire unused, which is precisely what the airline counted on.

The new bar downstairs has a sound system that shakes the floor of my apartment until two in the morning every weekend. The bar has a permit for music. The permit specifies decibel limits. The bar exceeds those limits routinely. The licensing board has been contacted. The licensing board says it will investigate, which is bureaucratic code for nothing will happen. I am being sonically assaulted on a schedule that the city has effectively approved.

Take me off your list. I have told you to take me off your list seventeen times. I am keeping a tally now. Each call from this number is added to the tally. The tally will be presented in court along with the federal Do Not Call complaint I have already filed against your company. Stop calling. Stop calling. Stop calling. I am not going to buy your product. I am not going to take a survey. I am not going to listen to your pitch.

Stop pretending you are a small family business when you have eleven locations, a private equity investor, and a marketing department staffed by twelve people. The family-owned-since aesthetic is a costume. The whole brand is a costume. And you are charging family-owned prices for corporate-margin products. The deception is offensive. Customers who care about supporting local should know exactly what they are actually supporting.

The streaming service raised prices for the fifth time in three years, added more ads to the plan that supposedly had no ads, and announced that password sharing would now incur an additional fee. They are charging more for less and they are doing it with the bored confidence of a company that knows its customers are too tired to leave. I am not too tired. I am canceling tonight and writing about it.

The locker room is overrun with men who insist on having full conversations naked in front of the lockers I need to open. They do not move. They do not pause. They continue blocking the lockers with their wet, unclothed bodies while I attempt to retrieve my belongings without making eye contact with anyone. The communal nudity is fine. The willingness to maintain a conference call atmosphere while being a physical obstruction is not.

The convenience store next to the disaster zone is selling flashlights for eighty dollars and gallons of water for thirty. They know the road is closed. They know the next store is forty miles down a flooded route. They have decided that desperation is a business opportunity. There is a special place reserved in public memory for this kind of behavior, and I intend to make sure it sticks.

If I hear that bass line one more time at one in the morning I am going to start banging on the wall with a baseball bat. We have asked. We have written notes. We have left voicemails. Every single weekend it is the same routine, the same throbbing wall, the same childish defiance from a thirty-five-year-old man who somehow has never learned what acceptable noise levels are. Grow up. Buy headphones. Move to the country if you cannot live with neighbors.

The email program decided that I meant to address the message to my CEO rather than to my colleague with the same first name. The CEO received my detailed complaint about the broken office coffee machine. The CEO does not handle coffee machines. The CEO now thinks I am the kind of employee who escalates appliance issues to the C-suite. My career may not survive this. The autocomplete has betrayed me utterly.

Imagine being so devoid of self-awareness that you log on to a forum dedicated to professional photographers and lecture them about exposure triangles because you watched one YouTube tutorial. The arrogance is staggering. Half the people you are condescending to have shot for magazines, taught classes, run studios. You should be reading their posts and taking notes, not correcting their grammar. Sit down before someone helps you sit down.

The clerk informed me that the form I filled out was the wrong form, that the correct form is available only at a different building across town, and that the office at that building closes in twenty minutes. She told me this in a tone that suggested I should have known. I did not know. I had no way of knowing. The signage on this building does not mention the other building. The website lists the wrong form. The system is broken and the clerk is enjoying the situation.

Every notification on my phone is a small theft of my attention by an algorithm designed by people who know exactly what they are doing. The engagement metrics. The infinite scroll. The carefully tuned outrage cycles. The whole apparatus is built to extract as many seconds of human consciousness as possible, and we have let them build it inside our pockets. I am genuinely furious at how willingly we surrendered.

The car insurance company raised my rates after another driver hit me. I did nothing wrong. The police report says so. The other driver's insurance paid out. And somehow my rates went up because the file shows I was involved in an accident. Involved. As the victim. The system is rigged against the people paying into it, and the regulators have either been bought off or fallen asleep. The whole thing is a slow-motion robbery.

He requested a status update on a task I started yesterday afternoon. The task is expected to take a week. He wants to know my progress, my obstacles, my next steps, and my projected completion date. He wants this in a spreadsheet, color-coded, with a written narrative attached. The task itself would have been half-finished by now if he had not interrupted me to demand a report on a task I have not had time to do because of the report demands.

The truck parked across two spaces is the universal symbol of selfishness in modern life. There is no excuse. There is no excuse. The driver is not too good for a single line. The truck is not too big for a normal space. The driver simply did not care, did not look, did not bother. And the rest of us spend an extra fifteen minutes circling the garage because of one man's refusal to participate in basic shared society.

The statement uses the passive voice with such consistency that you would not know a human being had ever made a decision at this company. Mistakes were made. Lessons were learned. Steps will be taken. Steps by whom. Taken in what direction. Walked by which executive between the boardroom and the helicopter. The whole document is a masterclass in the avoidance of moral agency by the people most responsible.

The newsletter signup overlay just asked me to wait, with a countdown, before I could close it. Wait. With a countdown. For five seconds. The site has decided that my time is worth precisely as little as it can extract by force. I refuse. I close the tab. I delete the link from my history. I will tell anyone who asks that this publication is not worth reading because of the experience of reading it, regardless of the actual content.

The agent demanded the original paper copy of a document the agency itself issued electronically. They have it. They sent it. I forwarded the email to her, in front of her, on her own screen. She still demanded a printed copy with an original signature. I am genuinely furious that the rules of this place have detached from the laws of physics, common sense, and the technological present. We do not live in 1973 anymore. Try to keep up.

This meeting could have been an email. This meeting could have been a Slack message. This meeting could have been a moment of silence followed by everyone going back to their actual jobs. Instead it is a forty-seven-minute affair in which fourteen people take turns saying they agree, with no decisions made, no actions assigned, and no follow-up scheduled except for another meeting next Tuesday at the same time.

The hotel voucher you offered me is for a property fifty miles from the airport. The shuttle stopped running at midnight. The Uber to get there will cost ninety dollars. The voucher is worth seventy dollars. So the compensation for ruining my evening is a net cost to me of twenty dollars and two hours of additional misery. This is not compensation. This is an insult dressed up as goodwill. I am keeping the receipt and submitting it to the DOT.

You raised my rent by twelve percent and have not fixed a single thing in this apartment for two years. The window does not close. The kitchen drawer is held together with duct tape. There is a permanent water stain on the ceiling shaped like an angry face that I have come to consider a roommate. You collect the check on the first of the month and then ghost every email until the next first of the month. This is not management. This is extortion.

Calling me at seven in the morning to ask if I want to switch my electricity provider is not a sales pitch. It is harassment. Do you have any idea how many people in this country work night shifts? Do you have any idea how many parents are trying to get their kids ready for school at this hour? No. Of course you do not. Because you are reading from a script written by someone who hates everyone, including you.

The driver delivered my package to the address two doors down. The neighbor is on vacation. The package is sitting on a stranger's porch. The tracking system shows it as delivered. The carrier insists I have to contact the recipient, who is unreachable. I am being told to walk into someone else's yard and retrieve the parcel myself, which the driver delivered incorrectly, and for which I will be blamed if anything goes wrong.

The self-checkout has been broken for the last fifteen minutes because the system thinks I did not bag an item that is in fact in the bag. The light is flashing red. The cashier monitoring six self-checkout stations is helping someone else. The attendant key is missing. The supervisor has not been called. I am standing here, paying customer, holding a basket, prevented from leaving by a robot that is wrong.

I do not need a thirty-minute meeting to discuss something that could be resolved in a two-sentence email. Stop scheduling pointless calls. Stop demanding face time as if you are paid by the minute of meeting attendance. Some of us are trying to do actual work over here, and your incessant calendar invites are a productivity tax I refuse to keep paying. Decline. Decline. Decline.

You have been wrong in this thread, and the previous thread, and the thread before that. Three for three. At some point the pattern stops being bad luck and starts being a deficiency. People are not piling on you. They are responding to a sustained campaign of misinformation that you keep refusing to acknowledge. Step away from the keyboard. Touch grass. Reconsider your relationship to confidence and accuracy.

Awards shows have become so insufferable that I would rather have a root canal than sit through one. The hosts are unfunny. The acceptance speeches are political lectures. The musical numbers are designed by committee. The whole spectacle is industry self-congratulation broadcast to the public so we can be reminded how unimportant we are. Turn it off. Read something. Take a walk. Do anything else.

The fact that we have allowed teenagers to grow up inside an attention slot machine designed by behavioral psychologists is going to be remembered as one of the worst collective decisions in modern history. The mental health data is catastrophic. The platform owners know it. They have known it for over a decade. They keep iterating to make the products more addictive, not less. And then they testify before Congress about how they are looking into it.

Reading the same paragraph back to me from your website does not constitute customer service. I have already read the website. I am calling because the website did not help. If you cannot do anything beyond recite text I could read myself, what exactly is the point of this conversation? End it. Hang up. Save us both the energy of pretending this is productive when both of us know it is theater.

The agent had the absolute gall to suggest that the broken product was somehow my fault for using it incorrectly. I plugged it in. That was the entire interaction. There is no incorrect way to plug something into a wall socket. Your product caught fire, and you are blaming the victim. The audacity is so dense it forms its own gravity well. I am taking my complaint public and I am taking it loud.

The strike zone in tonight's game was a moving target. Pitches in the dirt got called strikes. Pitches over the heart of the plate got called balls. The catcher kept looking at the home plate ump like he was watching a man invent a new sport in real time. Get the robot umps in. Now. I have lost all faith in the human eye to do this job consistently, and the players have too. The standard has collapsed.

Every new diet book is the same six chapters in a new cover. Cut sugar. Cut carbs. Cut whatever the previous decade said was healthy. Add whatever the previous decade said was bad. The cycle continues forever because there is more money in the next book than there is in admitting that the previous book was wrong. The authors know it. The publishers know it. The bookstores know it. We are the only ones still pretending this is science.

The flight crew has just informed us that they have timed out, that no replacement crew is available, and that the flight is canceled. They are leaving the aircraft. They are walking past us in their uniforms, on their phones, going home. We are still in our seats. We have been in our seats for four hours. We are now expected to deplane, retrieve our luggage, find a hotel, and start over tomorrow. The airline has provided no hotel. The airline has provided no taxi. The airline has provided nothing.

Approved colors. Approved fence styles. Approved roofing materials. Approved tree species. Approved holiday displays. Approved shrub heights. Approved mailbox flag positions. We are not living in homes. We are living inside a corporate brand guideline that some pencil-pusher invented in 1987. The whole point of homeownership was supposed to be that you could do what you wanted with your own house. That was the entire promise. We have been swindled.

Your app crashed during check-in. Your kiosk crashed at the airport. Your gate computer crashed during boarding. The only thing functioning reliably in your entire operation is the system that charges my credit card. Maybe invest some of those record profits into software that actually works instead of bonuses for the executives who designed this shambolic disaster of a travel experience. You should be embarrassed.

I clicked one button on the phone settings and was greeted with a six-step modal walking me through new features that I do not want, do not need, and cannot disable. Each screen requires me to tap continue to dismiss. The final screen offers no way to skip the rest of the tour. It is a hostage situation perpetrated by my own device. I have opted into nothing and yet here I am, captive, watching a slideshow about a search feature I will never use.

Whoever decided to put pineapple in the carbonara should be banned from kitchens for life. The bread was stale. The wine was vinegar. The owner came to the table and asked how everything was, and I had to bite my tongue so hard I tasted blood. This is the kind of restaurant that survives on tourist desperation and tripadvisor manipulation. A complete insult to the concept of hospitality.

Every time I scroll past a certain point on this recipe site a new video pops out from the bottom right corner, plays its first three seconds at full volume, then docks itself to the side of the screen so it can continue playing while I try to find the actual ingredient list. The ingredient list is one paragraph. The page is forty thousand words long. The food blogger has held it hostage behind a wall of self-indulgent prose and a SWAT team of video ads.

I mentioned, casually, that I had been a little tired lately, and a man I have known for forty-five minutes is now lecturing me about iron supplements, sleep hygiene, screen time, and the failures of modern medicine. I did not ask. I do not want his diagnosis. I want to finish my drink and go home. The unsolicited expertise is louder than the actual conversation. He has confused having strong opinions with being helpful.

The stadium parking lot wanted ninety dollars for a single event. The lot is a field. There are no attendants. There is no security. There is barely paint on the ground. They have erected a tollbooth, hired someone to point at parking spaces, and decided the experience of leaving your car on dirt for four hours is worth a hundred dollars. We parked six blocks away on a residential street and walked. Out of spite.

I do not have a car warranty. I have never had a car warranty. I do not own a car. I have explained this to every single one of you robotic vultures that has called me over the past eighteen months. Whatever list my number is on, it is wrong, and someone in your company should be paid to update it, although clearly no one is, because you keep calling, and I keep yelling, and we all keep wasting each other's lives.

I sat through four cycles of the same red light because the cross street had no one, no one, on it, and yet the timer kept telling me to wait. Modern traffic engineering is a humiliation. We can land probes on Mars but cannot get a light to turn green when there is nobody coming the other way. The wasted hours of human life at this single intersection alone are a moral crime.

The chatbot insisted I was looking for the wrong department for thirty minutes before finally allowing me to type the word human, after which it told me a human would call me back within forty-eight hours. Forty-eight hours. To answer a question your website could not. Whoever decided this system was acceptable customer service should be fired and forced to use it themselves. I would pay good money to watch.

Twenty-two flags in a single half. Twenty-two. The referees called more penalties than the players ran plays. The whole point of the game was buried under an avalanche of yellow flags and ten-minute pauses to review whether a finger touched a face mask. Let them play. Let the athletes do what they trained for. Stop interfering every six seconds because you are insecure about your own relevance to the broadcast.

The delivery driver took a photo of my package on the front step, then drove off with the package still in his truck. The photo is on my account. The package is not on my step. I watched on the doorbell camera as he held the package up, snapped the photo, and got back into the van with my parcel. He filed a successful delivery. I filed a complaint. The carrier sided with the driver because the photo proves delivery. The photo proves a lie, and I am furious that proof is now a participant in the deception.

The platform increased the price by forty percent and announced it via a footer link in a marketing email about new features. The new features are inferior versions of features that already existed and were taken away. The price increase is mandatory. The cancellation page is unreachable on mobile. The customer service line is closed. I am, in every meaningful sense, being held hostage by a company that started as a startup with a feel-good origin story I no longer believe.

Every email I send out is copied to him for approval. Every line of code I push is reviewed line by line by him personally. Every decision I make is overruled, sometimes hours later, in a way that requires me to redo work. He is not a manager. He is a bottleneck with a salary. The team has stopped trying to be efficient because he will undo any efficiency we create. We are paid to do nothing while looking busy.

The flashlight app wants access to my contacts, my microphone, my location, my calendar, and my photo library. It is a flashlight. It turns on the LED. It does not need to know who my friends are. It does not need to know where I am. It does not need to listen to me. The permission requests are not for the functionality of the flashlight. The permission requests are for the data harvest. The app is a vehicle for surveillance disguised as a utility.

The form will not let me proceed because my password contains a special character. It then refuses to let me proceed without a special character. The two rules are mutually exclusive. There is no combination of characters that satisfies the validation logic. I have tried for twenty minutes. I have invented passwords of increasing eccentricity. The system has rejected all of them. I am locked out of an account I created today, by rules that contradict themselves, on a platform that does not respond to support requests.

Eight forms. I had to fill out eight forms to renew a license that the same office issued me five years ago. They already have my information. They already have my photograph. They have a literal database with my name in it. And yet here I am, in the same chair I sat in last time, copying the same information onto the same forms, while the same clerk stares at me with the same dead eyes. Why do we accept this?

The customer ahead of me is paying for two hundred dollars of groceries with exact change in pennies. The cashier is patient. The customer is methodical. The line behind us has stopped being a line and has become a small protest movement. I am eight minutes into this transaction and the change is being counted twice because the cashier wants to be sure. I am being held hostage by a coin avalanche.

Your service has been out for nine consecutive hours and your support bot keeps asking me to verify the four lights on my modem. Three of the lights are off because the service is off. The fourth light is blinking red, which I am told indicates that your equipment has given up on life. Send a human. Send anyone. I do not need to be patronized by an automated message at four in the morning when I am trying to file a refund claim.

The update broke the printer driver. The printer is now a paperweight. The driver is no longer available from the manufacturer because the printer is six years old, which the printer industry classifies as antediluvian. The replacement printers all require a subscription to use ink they sell at the price of fine champagne. The entire economy is engineered to discard functional equipment in the name of progress and I have had enough.

The deepfake scams targeting CEOs are a preview of what is coming for the rest of us. Already there are calls from people who sound exactly like family members asking for emergency wires. Already there are videos of executives saying things they never said. Already the trust foundation of modern communication is dissolving. And the response from the platforms enabling this is a polite shrug. Disgraceful.

I am required to submit an architectural review form to change the color of my front door. To change the color. Of my own front door. On my own property. That I own. The form costs fifty dollars to file. The review takes six weeks. The committee meets once a month and the next meeting is in two months. I am painting the door this weekend regardless of what they say. I will pay the fine. I will fight the fine. I will not be ruled by a board of paint inspectors.

The stranger at the playground has informed me that my child is dressed too warmly, that I am holding her wrong, that the snack I gave her is not nutritious, and that her shoe is on the incorrect foot. The shoe is on the correct foot. I checked. I am holding my child. I have been holding her for three years. The stranger is a retired teacher, which she has mentioned twice in the first minute, and the credential has apparently licensed her to deliver parenting reviews unsolicited.

Three lanes closed for construction and not a single worker in sight. Not one. Not a hard hat, not a backhoe, not a guy holding a sign. Just orange cones stretching to the horizon and forty thousand cars crawling through at five miles an hour for absolutely no apparent reason. Whoever planned this should be put in stocks in the town square. The contempt for human time is staggering.

The phone autocompleted my apology into something insulting. I typed I am so sorry and the phone suggested I am so sorry you are like this. I did not see the change before pressing send. The recipient has not responded. The recipient may not respond for a long time. The autocomplete has, in a single act, ended a friendship that took fifteen years to build, and the company that programmed it has a market cap larger than several small nations.

The customer service line transferred me to four departments, each one insisting they did not handle my type of claim, before disconnecting me when the call was finally routed to the right place. Forty-seven minutes of my life consumed. No resolution. Just a long lesson in how this company avoids paying out by burying its own paying customers in process. The cruelty is calculated. It is line-item in the quarterly budget.

Forced reboot. Forced reboot. Forced reboot. Three forced reboots in one afternoon, each preceded by a banner that promised the update would only take a few minutes. The few minutes have stretched to nearly two hours of unproductive waiting. The screen has cycled through configuration progress indicators that mean nothing to me. I cannot work. I cannot save. I cannot do anything but watch a circular animation rotate while the company that took my money slowly defaces my computer.

There is sweat on the bench. There is sweat on the floor. There is sweat on the handles of the rowing machine. The previous user has left an absolute biological deposit on every surface he touched, and the wipes the gym provides are six aisles away because the dispenser nearest us was emptied three days ago and not refilled. The signs everywhere instruct us to wipe down equipment. The previous user has clearly never read a sign in his life.

The fitness app does not need my contacts. The fitness app should not have my contacts. The fitness app has, somehow, my contacts. It is suggesting that I add friends from my address book to its social platform, which I did not sign up for, and which I do not want. I revoked the contacts permission. The app remembered the contacts anyway, because the data was already uploaded to their servers. The permission revocation is performance. The harvest already happened.

I work from home. I pay you over two hundred dollars a month for the privilege of being told to restart my router every time the service drops, which is roughly forty times since Tuesday. The router has been restarted so often it has developed feelings. The cables are immaculate. The modem is begging for retirement. The problem is on your end and the fact that I have to perform this charade every single time is an absolute disgrace.

The food finally arrived after an hour and twenty minutes and it was lukewarm, picked at by whoever ferried it through the corridor, and missing the side dish that was its only redeeming feature on the menu. When I pointed this out the server informed me that the kitchen was unusually busy. Three tables. Three. The kitchen was not busy. The kitchen was indifferent, which is worse.

Step therapy is just sadism wearing a clipboard. I have been on a medication that works for me for eight years. The insurance company has decided I need to fail on two cheaper alternatives before they will cover what I am already taking. They want me to get sicker, to prove I cannot tolerate the cheap stuff, before they will pay for the expensive stuff. The whole premise is bankrupt. The whole industry needs to be torn down.

The check took longer to arrive than the entrees, which is impressive given that the entrees took an hour. When I finally flagged someone down they brought the wrong check, then took another fifteen minutes to bring the correct one, and then disappeared again with my card for so long I genuinely considered whether I had been the victim of a stealth dine and dash from the staff side.

He drove over the lawn. The lawn now has two deep tire ruts where the grass used to be. The driveway was clear. There was no obstruction. He chose, deliberately, to take a shortcut through landscaping I have spent two summers cultivating. When I called the company, they said the driver denies any contact with the lawn. The doorbell video shows the tires, the lawn, and the trajectory. Denial is the only tool they have left.

An autoplay video for car insurance just started screaming at full volume from a tab I cannot find. I have eleven tabs open. The ad is in one of them. I am tabbing through frantically while my baby sleeps in the next room. The volume control on the ad does not work because the player is custom, branded, and apparently engineered specifically to inflict maximum disruption. I am closing the browser. I am closing the laptop. I am throwing the laptop into the sea.

There are eighteen registers in this store. Two of them are open. The line stretches back into the frozen aisle. The manager is standing at the front, holding a clipboard, watching customers seethe. He is not opening more registers. He is not bagging items. He is not doing anything but observing the disaster he has personally caused by understaffing on a Saturday afternoon. I have been in line for twenty-three minutes for a single carton of milk.

The technician scheduled to come Tuesday between eight and noon arrived on Thursday at four in the afternoon, told me the issue was outside my house and beyond his scope, and left. The issue is still there. The next available appointment is in eleven days. Eleven days. I am supposed to live without internet for eleven days because your scheduling system is a joke and your technicians can apparently invent new categories of unfixable problem at will.

The owner came over after the meal to ask how everything was, and I gave him both barrels. He nodded sympathetically and offered us a free dessert. We had been here three hours. The last thing anyone in this party wanted was to spend another twenty minutes waiting for a tiramisu. He did not understand. He genuinely did not understand. That is the problem, and that is why this place will be empty in a year.

Every red carpet event has become an exercise in unbearable smugness, with celebrities pretending the dress they were paid to wear is a political statement, and journalists asking softball questions like they were granted an audience with the pope. The whole industry feeds on its own self-importance and expects the rest of us to applaud the performance. I will not applaud. I will turn off the broadcast and read a book instead.

The HOA fines a single mother sixty dollars for letting her grass grow half an inch over the limit, while the board president has a junked car on his lawn for three months and pays no fine. The selective enforcement is so blatant it is almost performance art. The board protects its own. The board harasses everyone else. The board needs to be voted out, and I have started collecting signatures already.

The comments section is now ninety-five percent bots, five percent enraged humans, and zero percent anything resembling thoughtful conversation. Every post about anything attracts the same six insults from the same dozen accounts that all opened in 2024 and have never posted anything else. The platform knows this is happening. The platform does nothing about it. Because the bot engagement counts in the ad metrics, and the truth is just expensive.

The popup wants my email. The popup wants my phone number. The popup wants my zip code. The popup wants my age range. The popup wants my income bracket. The popup wants my opinion on three unrelated products. The popup will not close until I provide at least three of these. The popup is a phishing operation dressed up as a subscription form, and the site is hosting it without apology.

Stop demonizing entire categories of food. Carbs are not the enemy. Fat is not the enemy. The enemy is the marketing machine that has convinced everyone they need to be in a perpetual war with their own dinner. I refuse to live in fear of bread. I refuse to spend my life calculating macros. And I refuse to give one more dollar to the diet industrial complex that thrives on making humans hate themselves.

The acquaintance at the dinner party has decided that I would benefit from her unsolicited wisdom on my dating life, my financial decisions, my exercise habits, and my food choices, despite the fact that I have not asked for any of this and have given no indication of welcoming the feedback. She has positioned herself as a guru. She is a real estate agent. The advice is generic, dated, and faintly insulting. I am counting the minutes until I can excuse myself.

Every female character exists solely to be rescued, mourned, or kissed by a male character. It is twenty-five and the writing room apparently still has not been told. The romance has the chemistry of a damp paper towel. The comedy relies on the same tired stereotypes I thought we collectively retired a decade ago. The whole movie is a fossil pretending to be cutting-edge cinema. Embarrassing.

The restaurant added an automatic gratuity to a party of four, which is two below their stated party-size threshold for automatic gratuity. When questioned, the manager said it was an oversight and could be removed, then deducted only half. The remaining half stayed on the bill as a separate line item with no explanation. I tipped on top of this because I am a coward in restaurant settings, and now I am writing an angry review at home, where bravery is cheap.

I asked you to stop using my name as if we are old friends. I asked you to identify your company. I asked you to confirm I am on a recorded line. You ignored all three requests and continued your pitch. That tells me everything I need to know about whether this is a legitimate business call or a predatory operation hoping to catch someone tired enough to give in. I am not tired enough. Hang up. Click. Goodbye.

I muted the tab. The ad unmuted itself. I muted it again. It unmuted itself again. I muted my entire system. The ad found a way around the system mute and continued playing. I closed the laptop. The browser is now haunted. The ad has clearly transcended the boundaries of polite digital existence and is now an entity in its own right, pursuing me through cyberspace, demanding that I learn about a refinance program I would not consider if my life depended on it.

Wipe down the bench. Wipe it. You sweated through three sets of incline press and then walked away without touching the spray bottle six feet to your left. The next person to use that bench is now sitting in your perspiration. This is disgusting. This is rude. This is the kind of behavior that gets you reported to the front desk every single time, and I have been reporting it, because civilization runs on basic hygiene.
